title: Prediction-Powered Risk Monitoring of Deployed Models for Detecting Harmful Distribution Shifts
one_liner: Monitor whether a deployed model's error rate has become dangerously high by mixing many synthetic labels with a small stream of true labels and keeping a valid running lower bound on risk.
lead: A deployed model can degrade after launch because the input distribution changes. The direct way to detect that is to keep collecting labels and recomputing risk, but labels are expensive and often delayed. The paper proposes prediction-powered risk monitoring, which uses synthetic labels from an auxiliary predictor together with a small amount of true labeled data. The output is an anytime-valid lower bound on the current running risk, meaning a bound that remains statistically valid no matter when the monitoring process is stopped. Harmful shift is flagged when that lower bound crosses a nominal-risk threshold, so the system can detect worsening performance without waiting for dense labels.

problem.h2: After deployment, labels arrive slowly but harm can arrive quickly
paras: A classifier can look safe on validation data and then fail once real traffic shifts. New subpopulations may appear, the prevalence of hard cases may rise, or prompt style may change for a language model. If the team waits for a large labeled audit, harmful behavior can persist for too long.

Purely unlabeled monitoring has the opposite weakness. It can detect that inputs look different, but not whether the model's actual loss has crossed a harmful threshold. The paper focuses on the more direct question: can we monitor running risk itself when true labels are scarce, using synthetic labels only as a variance-reduction aid rather than as a substitute for correctness?

callout.html: Use predictions to stretch a small label budget into a valid risk alarm, because synthetic labels can sharpen estimation when a few real labels keep them anchored.

steps.text: Collect model outputs on incoming data and maintain a running estimate of risk, because the target is ongoing post-deployment loss.
Use an auxiliary predictor to approximate labels for many examples, because broad approximate coverage can reduce the variance of the risk estimate.

steps.b: Correct with a small set of true labels.
steps.text: Use the real labels to debias or calibrate the prediction-powered estimate, because synthetic labels alone are not trusted as ground truth.
Update a lower confidence bound on the running risk that stays valid under continuous monitoring, because the operator may stop and inspect the bound at any time.

steps.b: Compare against the nominal-risk upper bound.
steps.text: Flag harmful shift when the monitored lower bound exceeds what was acceptable under nominal conditions, because then the bad-risk conclusion is already supported by finite-sample evidence.

paras: The paper changes deployment monitoring from raw drift detection into direct sequential monitoring of model risk with finite-sample false-alarm control.

hidden.name: running post-deployment risk under scarce labels
paras: The hidden quantity is the cumulative or running error rate the deployed model is currently incurring on the live stream. That is the quantity operators care about, but it is only partially observed because true labels appear slowly.

Prediction-powered monitoring makes that hidden quantity more visible by borrowing structure from synthetic labels while forcing every alarm to remain anchored to the real labels. The lower bound is the important object. It asks not what the best estimate of risk is, but what risk level is already justified with high confidence at the current time.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the pieces needed to turn sparse labels into a valid online risk alarm.

reads.html: The monitor is trying to prove that the model's live error rate is already too high, even before many labels arrive.
PPRM tracks a prediction-powered lower confidence bound on running risk, so the alarm is based on a quantity that remains valid under optional stopping and repeated looks at the data.

paras: Synthetic labels help only if they are used carefully, because on their own they can be badly biased under distribution shift. The paper uses them as a control variate, meaning an auxiliary signal that reduces noise in the estimate, while the real labels provide the correction that keeps the monitored quantity tied to actual risk.

The anytime-valid lower bound matters because monitoring is sequential. In deployment, one does not decide in advance to check only after exactly 5,000 examples. Teams watch dashboards continuously. Ordinary fixed-sample confidence intervals can give too many false alarms under that behavior. An anytime-valid bound is built to survive repeated checking.

The threshold comparison is also asymmetric in a useful way. The monitor constructs a lower bound on current risk and compares it with an upper bound on nominal risk. That means an alarm only fires when the evidence is strong enough to say the current system is already worse than the acceptable baseline, which controls type-I error because the bad-risk conclusion is required to clear both uncertainty bands rather than only one point estimate.

math.words: Raise an alarm once the monitored lower bound on current running risk rises above the accepted upper bound for nominal risk.
symbols: the anytime-valid lower confidence bound on the deployed model's running risk after prediction-powered correction
the accepted upper confidence bound for the model's risk under nominal conditions
the decision to flag a harmful distribution shift for intervention or review

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the nominal system was accepted with an upper risk bound of 0.08.
The live monitor uses synthetic labels on 10,000 cases and true labels on 200 of them.
After correction, the current lower risk bound is only 0.05, so no alarm fires yet.
Later, after more shifted traffic and a few more true labels, the lower bound rises to 0.10.
Now the lower bound exceeds the nominal upper bound, so the monitor can flag harmful shift with controlled false-alarm risk.

math.note: The rule is conservative in the right direction: it waits until bad current risk is already supported by evidence.

charts.title: Unlabeled drift monitor

charts.title: Prediction-powered risk monitor
charts.note: The method works because synthetic labels provide coverage while true labels keep the alarm tied to real risk.

items.b: Synthetic labels can become very poor under severe shift.
items.html: If the auxiliary predictor fails badly on the shifted traffic, variance reduction may weaken or even reverse, because the correction terms must work harder to repair the bad approximation.

items.b: Too few true labels can delay alarms.
items.html: The procedure controls false alarms, but it still needs some real labels to tighten the lower bound, so detection may remain slow when supervision is extremely scarce.
If the accepted nominal-risk bound was itself poorly estimated, the alarm threshold may be miscalibrated from the start.

The method is most useful when teams need a risk-based deployment alarm under sparse labels, because it converts prediction coverage plus limited supervision into a statistically grounded monitoring rule.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Simulate a deployed classifier where the test distribution shifts halfway through the stream. Provide synthetic labels for every example from an auxiliary model and true labels for only a small random subset. Compare three monitors: raw input drift, a label-only running risk estimate, and prediction-powered risk monitoring.

The demo should report detection delay and false alarms under continuous monitoring. A convincing result is that the prediction-powered monitor alarms earlier than the label-only monitor while keeping interpretable false-alarm control, because the synthetic labels reduce noise and the real labels keep the bound valid.
demo.closing: The practical win is a deployment alarm that speaks in terms of risk rather than only in terms of changed inputs.
